summary: Describes a mechanism for automatic discovery and creation of IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnels using extensions to multiprotocol BGP, so IPv4 networks can connect across an IPv6 backbone. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Two old-style networks are separated by a new-style one. This builds a tunnel through the middle so they can still talk, and the routers find each other automatically.

questions: how to connect ipv4 networks across an ipv6 backbone
how does automatic tunnel discovery work in 4over6
subtitle: Connecting IPv4 islands across an IPv6 backbone automatically

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks are being deployed, but IPv4 networks still need to communicate. An IPv6 backbone cannot directly route IPv4 packets.
tldr.mechanism: 4over6 uses dual-stack PE routers at the network edge to encapsulate IPv4 packets in IPv6 headers and automatically discovers tunnel endpoints using MP-BGP extensions.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 networks can exchange traffic across IPv6 backbones without manual tunnel configuration.

today: RFC 5747 is an Experimental specification. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and represents a practical approach to IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling that was implemented and deployed in China.

sections.title: Why IPv4 over IPv6
sections.content: IPv6 networks are being deployed as backbones to replace aging IPv4 infrastructure, but countless applications and hosts still require IPv4. Rather than wait for complete migration, network operators need a way for separate IPv4 networks to communicate across an IPv6-only backbone. The standard approach of manually configuring tunnels does not scale well across many edge routers, so automatic discovery is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: When you have an old thing and a new thing, sometimes you build a bridge so they can both work at the same time.

sections.title: The 4over6 Architecture
sections.content: The 4over6 system has several layers. An IPv6 backbone connects multiple Provider Edge (PE) routers, which are dual-stack devices. Each PE router connects to one or more IPv4 access networks. The core P routers in the backbone run IPv6 only. When an IPv4 packet arrives at an ingress PE router destined for a remote IPv4 network, the PE router encapsulates the entire IPv4 packet inside an IPv6 header and sends it across the backbone. The egress PE router removes the IPv6 header and delivers the original IPv4 packet to its destination. From the perspective of the backbone, these are just normal IPv6 packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A PE router is like a translator that wraps an old-style message in new-style packaging so it can travel through the modern network.

sections.title: How 4over6 Routing Works
sections.content: Each 4over6 PE router maintains an encapsulation table that maps IPv4 destination prefixes to the IPv6 virtual interface (VIF) address of the PE router that reaches those prefixes. The ingress PE learns these mappings through MP-BGP (Multiprotocol BGP) with a new SAFI (Subsequent Address Family Identifier) value of 67 assigned for 4over6 traffic. When a PE router learns a local IPv4 prefix from its access network, it advertises that prefix along with its own IPv6 VIF address to all other PE routers. This enables each PE to know exactly where to send IPv4 traffic destined for any reachable prefix. Because the routing information is exchanged via BGP, tunnel endpoints are discovered automatically without manual configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Each translator keeps a list: this old-style address lives at that translator (by their new-style address). When a message arrives, the translator looks up where it should go and sends it there.

sections.title: Packet Forwarding and Encapsulation
sections.content: When an IPv4 packet arrives at an ingress PE router, the router performs a lookup in its local IPv4 routing table to find the matching prefix in the encapsulation table. This lookup yields the IPv6 VIF address of the egress PE router. The ingress PE then wraps the entire IPv4 packet in an IPv6 header, using its own IPv6 VIF address as the source and the egress PE's IPv6 VIF address as the destination. The IPv6 header uses the encapsulation format defined in RFC 2473 (IP encapsulation in IPv6). The P routers in the backbone treat this as a standard IPv6 packet and forward it using normal IPv6 routing. When the encapsulated packet reaches the egress PE router, that router removes the IPv6 header and forwards the original IPv4 packet to its destination using the local IPv4 routing table.
sections.plainLanguage: A message comes in wrapped as old-style. The ingress translator wraps it as new-style with delivery instructions, sends it through the network, and the egress translator unwraps it back to old-style.

sections.title: Real-World Deployment
sections.content: A prototype implementation was developed and deployed on CNGI-CERNET2, the China Next Generation Internet backbone operated by the China Education and Research Network. CNGI-CERNET2 connects approximately 25 core nodes across 20 Chinese cities at speeds of 2.5 to 10 Gb/s and is IPv6-only at the core. The prototype was implemented as Linux kernel modules for packet forwarding and encapsulation, with MP-BGP extensions developed in Zebra routing software. Testing confirmed that IPv4 packets successfully transit the IPv6 backbone. The deployment tested HTTP downloads, peer-to-peer file sharing, FTP, SSH, instant messaging and multimedia streaming, all functioning correctly across the IPv6 backbone.
sections.plainLanguage: A real system was built and tested at several universities across China. It worked for downloading files, chatting, video, and other applications.
